title: 5 ways to deal with questions that have multiple correct answers
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton takes up a practical problem with learner-generated-example questions: when many answers are correct (or incorrect), checking the whole class's understanding by cold call or mini-whiteboard is slow and unreliable. He opens with two observed lessons in which the teacher either faced a sea of hands asking whether their own answer was also right or missed wrong answers scattered across 30 boards. He then offers five responses: place these questions deliberately, adapt them to a single answer, use Adam Boxer's collect-and-predict method, run structured peer assessment, and use the Give an example of... framework. The move throughout is to keep the rich thinking such questions provoke while cutting the assessment cost. The piece is a compact, classroom-ready set of techniques rather than a research argument.
points: Open-ended example-generation questions are excellent for discussion but should be kept out of the Do Now, where checking many valid answers wrecks the short, snappy start.
Tightening constraints (a specific numerator, or a value between two bounds) converts a many-answer question into one that is quick to check.
Adam Boxer's method pre-empts questions by writing up correct and predicted incorrect answers and having students star anything unlisted to ask about while he circulates.
Peer assessment with ticks for certain answers and stars for doubtful ones gives students a way to resolve disagreements, though shared misconceptions can slip through.
The Give an example of... frame asks for multiple examples, a boundary example and a plausible non-example, which structures what there is to assess.

You want the start of the lesson to be short and snappy, and if you find you need to take a relatively long time checking the understanding of a certain question because it has multiple possible correct answers, then you may find that portion of the lesson begins to unravel.

Most questions with multiple answers can be adapted so there is only one correct answer. In the equivalent fractions example, students could be tasked with finding equivalent fractions with specific numerators or denominators.

He then tells his students that if they have a different answer and they are not sure whether it is right or wrong to put a star by it and ask him whilst he is circulating during the lesson. This stops Adam from having to deal with a load of questions in the moment.

Of course, this approach does not guarantee a wrong answer will not slip through the net - after all, both students might share the same misconceptions - but I find it does catch most issues, and those starred questions always provide a fertile catalyst for whole-class discussions.
